A content delivery network solves a simple problem: a website's home base might sit on a single machine, called the origin server, located far from many of the people trying to reach it. Every request that travels all the way to that distant origin server takes time, and if thousands of people ask at once, things slow down or break. So a content delivery network scatters copies of the website's content across many computers placed in cities all over the world, known as edge locations. When someone requests a page, the network sends them to the nearest edge location instead of the faraway origin. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood bakeries stocking the same bread recipe from a central kitchen, so nobody has to drive across the country for a loaf. If the nearby edge location already has a saved copy of what's needed, that's called a cache hit, and the content delivers almost instantly, without ever contacting the origin server. Only when nothing is cached nearby does the request travel back to the source, fetch the content, and store a copy closer by for next time. The result is faster loading, less strain on the origin server, and a smoother experience even during huge traffic spikes.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing the real, master copy of a website | It's the ultimate source of truth when nothing else has the content |
| Edge location | A smaller server placed close to everyday users | It shortens the physical distance data has to travel |
| Cache hit | A successful match where nearby stored content answers a request | It means near-instant delivery with no long trip needed |
| Latency | The delay between asking for something and receiving it | Lower delay makes browsing feel fast and effortless |
